summary: Signs, traffic signals, and lines on the pavement tell you how to drive before you reach a hazard. This chapter covers what sign colors and shapes mean, how to respond to steady and flashing lights and arrows, and how to read yellow and white lines on the road.

Color tells you a lot even before you can read the words. Red is used for stop, yield, and do not enter. Yellow warns of a hazard ahead, orange marks road work, and fluorescent yellow-green is used for schools, people walking, and bicycles. White signs state rules you must obey, green signs give directions, blue signs point to services, and brown signs lead to parks and recreation.

Shape helps too. The red eight-sided sign always means stop, and the red and white triangle pointing down always means yield. The five-sided sign means a school zone or school crossing. The round yellow sign warns that a railroad crossing is ahead, and the white X-shaped crossbuck at the tracks should be treated like a yield sign.

Traffic signals and pavement markings finish the picture. A flashing red light means the same as a stop sign, and a flashing yellow light means slow down and go with care. A flashing yellow arrow lets you turn only after you yield. Yellow lines separate traffic moving in opposite directions, white lines separate lanes moving the same way, and a double solid yellow line means no passing in either direction.

concepts.definition: Red: stop, yield, do not enter. Yellow: general warning. Orange: work zone. Fluorescent yellow-green: school, pedestrian, and bicycle warnings. White: rules you must obey. Green: directions and distances. Blue: services for drivers. Brown: parks and recreation.
concepts.tip: Red stops you, yellow warns you, white rules you, green guides you.

source.org: Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (FHWA)

concepts.definition: A red eight-sided sign means come to a full stop and go only when it is safe. A red and white triangle pointing down means slow down and let traffic and pedestrians go first, stopping if you need to.
concepts.tip: Eight sides: stop all the way. Triangle pointing down: give way.

concepts.term: DO NOT ENTER and WRONG WAY
concepts.definition: A red circle with a white bar means you must not drive into that road or ramp from your direction. A red WRONG WAY sign means you are driving against traffic and must turn around safely.
concepts.tip: Red and white at a ramp: this is not your way in.

concepts.definition: A round yellow sign with an X and two R letters warns that a railroad crossing is ahead. At the tracks, the white X-shaped crossbuck should be treated like a yield sign: slow down, look and listen, and be ready to stop for a train.
concepts.tip: Round sign: railroad ahead. X-shaped crossbuck: you are at the tracks.

concepts.definition: A flashing red light means the same as a stop sign. A flashing yellow light means slow down and go with care. A flashing yellow arrow allows a turn only after you yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians. If signals are dark, treat the intersection like a four-way stop.
concepts.tip: Flashing red acts like a stop sign. Flashing yellow means caution.

source.org: Illinois Rules of the Road (Illinois Secretary of State)

concepts.definition: Yellow lines separate traffic going in opposite directions. White lines separate lanes going in the same direction. You may pass across a broken line on your side when it is safe, but not across a solid line on your side. A double solid yellow line means no passing in either direction.
concepts.tip: Yellow means oncoming traffic is on the other side of the line.

source.org: Illinois Rules of the Road (Illinois Secretary of State)

points: Red signs mean stop, yield, or do not enter.
Yellow means warning, orange means road work, and white means a rule you must obey.
The five-sided sign means a school zone or school crossing.
Treat a railroad crossbuck like a yield sign.
A flashing red light means the same as a STOP sign.
A double solid yellow line means no passing in either direction.

figures.alt: Eight color swatches in two rows, each labeled: red for stop, yield, do not enter; yellow for a hazard ahead; orange for road work; yellow-green for school, people walking, bikes; white for a rule you must obey; green for directions; blue for services; brown for parks.
figures.caption: Each sign color has its own job, so you can tell what a sign is about before you read it.

summary: Right of way rules decide who goes first when two road users want the same space. This chapter covers four-way stops, intersections without signs, turns, roundabouts, and the times when you must stop or yield for pedestrians, emergency vehicles, school buses, and trains.

At a four-way stop, the first vehicle to stop goes first. If two vehicles arrive at the same time, the driver on the left yields to the driver on the right, and the same rule applies at intersections with no signs or signals. When you turn left on a plain green light, yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians. You may turn right on red after a full stop unless a sign forbids it. At a roundabout, yield to traffic already in the circle.

Some road users always get special care. Yield to pedestrians in crosswalks, and stop before the sidewalk when you leave a driveway or alley. For an emergency vehicle using a siren and flashing lights, pull to the right edge of the road and stop. Under Scott's Law, when you approach a stopped emergency vehicle with flashing lights, change to a lane away from it if you safely can, or slow down and pass with care.

For a school bus with red lights flashing and its stop arm out, traffic going both ways must stop on a two-lane road. On a highway with 4 or more lanes and at least 2 lanes going each way, traffic going the opposite direction does not have to stop. At a railroad crossing with flashing signals, a lowered gate, a flagger, or a train close by, stop within 50 feet but not less than 15 feet from the nearest rail.

concepts.definition: Every vehicle must stop. The first vehicle to stop goes first. If two arrive at the same time, the driver on the left yields to the driver on the right.
concepts.tip: First come, first served. A tie goes to the driver on the right.

source.org: Illinois Rules of the Road (Illinois Secretary of State)

concepts.definition: On a plain green light, a left turn must yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians. A right turn on red is allowed after a full stop unless a sign forbids it, and you must yield first.
concepts.tip: Stop, look, yield, then turn.

concepts.definition: For an emergency vehicle using a siren and flashing lights, pull to the right edge of the road and stop until it passes. Do not stop inside an intersection.
concepts.tip: Hear a siren: pull right and stop.

concepts.definition: When you approach a stopped emergency vehicle with flashing lights, go with due care. Change to a lane that is not next to it if you can do so safely. If not, slow down and pass with care.
concepts.tip: Move over, or slow down.

concepts.definition: When a school bus stops with red lights flashing and the stop arm out, stop and stay stopped until the lights stop and the arm is pulled back. On a highway with 4 or more lanes and at least 2 lanes going each way, traffic going the opposite direction does not have to stop.
concepts.tip: Red lights on a bus: stop, unless a 4-lane highway puts you on the other side.

concepts.definition: When signals flash, a gate is down, a flagger signals, or a train is close, stop within 50 feet but not less than 15 feet from the nearest rail, and go only when it is safe.
concepts.tip: Stop between 15 and 50 feet from the tracks.

points: At a four-way stop, the first to stop goes first.
If two arrive together, yield to the driver on the right.
Pull right and stop for a siren and flashing lights.
Under Scott's Law, move over or slow down for a stopped emergency vehicle.
On a 4-lane highway, traffic going the other way need not stop for a school bus.
Stop 15 to 50 feet from the nearest rail when a train is coming.

compare.title: Who stops for a stopped school bus
rows: Highway with 4 or more lanes (at least 2 each way)
No need to stop, but watch for children

summary: This chapter covers Illinois speed limits, how to pass safely, and the places where you may not park. Many questions use exact numbers, so learn them together.

When no other limit is posted, the Illinois speed limit is 30 mph in an urban district, 15 mph in an alley, and 55 mph on most other highways. Some highways, such as interstates, have higher posted limits. In a school zone, the limit is 20 mph on school days when children are present. The posted limit is for good conditions, so drive slower in snow, rain, fog, or heavy traffic.
Pass on the left, and only where you can see far enough ahead. Never pass on a hill or curve where you cannot see oncoming traffic. When someone is passing you, stay in your lane and do not speed up.

Do not park within 15 feet of a fire hydrant, within 20 feet of a crosswalk at an intersection, within 30 feet of a stop sign, yield sign, or traffic signal on the side you approach from, or within 50 feet of the nearest rail of a railroad crossing. Stay at least 20 feet from a fire station driveway on the same side of the street. When you park downhill next to a curb, turn your wheels toward the curb.

concepts.definition: When no other limit is posted: 30 mph in an urban district, 15 mph in an alley, and 55 mph on most other highways.
concepts.tip: Town 30, alley 15, open road 55.

concepts.definition: The limit is 20 mph in a school zone on school days when children are present.
concepts.tip: Kids around the school: 20 mph.

concepts.definition: The posted limit is the most you may drive in good conditions. In bad weather or heavy traffic, drive slower so you can stop safely.
concepts.tip: The limit is a maximum, not a target.

concepts.definition: Pass on the left, and only when you can see far enough ahead. Do not pass on hills or curves. When you are being passed, keep your lane and do not speed up.
concepts.tip: Can't see ahead? Don't pass.

concepts.definition: Do not park within 15 feet of a fire hydrant, 20 feet of a crosswalk at an intersection, 30 feet of a stop sign or traffic signal on the approach side, 50 feet of the nearest rail of a railroad crossing, or 20 feet of a fire station driveway on the same side.
concepts.tip: 15 hydrant, 20 crosswalk, 30 stop sign, 50 railroad.

concepts.definition: Facing downhill next to a curb, turn your front wheels toward the curb and set the parking brake.
concepts.tip: Downhill: wheels to the curb.

points: Urban district default: 30 mph.
Alley: 15 mph. Most other highways: 55 mph unless posted.
School zone: 20 mph on school days when children are present.
Never pass on a hill or curve you cannot see past.
No parking within 15 feet of a hydrant or 20 feet of a crosswalk.
No parking within 30 feet of a stop sign or 50 feet of a railroad crossing.

compare.title: No parking distances
rows: Stop sign, yield sign, or traffic signal (approach side)
Nearest rail of a railroad crossing

summary: Safe driving is about seeing, being seen, and leaving yourself room to react. This chapter covers turn signals, headlights, following distance, bad weather, work zones, sharing the road, and phones.

Signal continuously for at least the last 100 feet before a turn or lane change in a business or residence district, and at least 200 feet elsewhere. Before changing lanes, check your mirrors and turn your head to check your blind spot. Give motorcycles a full lane.

Turn on your headlights from sunset to sunrise, whenever rain, snow, or fog makes you use your windshield wipers, and whenever you cannot clearly see people and vehicles 1,000 feet ahead. Parking lights may be used with headlights but never instead of them. Dim your high beams within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle and within 300 feet of a vehicle you are following.

On wet roads, leave more following distance. If you hydroplane, ease off the gas and steer straight. In work zones, slow down and obey signs and flaggers. Illinois bans using a hand-held phone while driving, so put the phone away.

concepts.definition: Signal continuously for at least the last 100 feet before turning or changing lanes in a business or residence district, and at least 200 feet outside those districts.
concepts.tip: Town 100 feet, open road 200 feet.

concepts.definition: From sunset to sunrise, when weather makes you use windshield wipers, and when people and vehicles are not clearly visible 1,000 feet ahead. Parking lights may not replace headlights.
concepts.tip: Wipers on, lights on.

concepts.definition: Dim high beams within 500 feet of a vehicle coming toward you and within 300 feet of a vehicle you are following.
concepts.tip: 500 oncoming, 300 following.

concepts.definition: Illinois bans using a hand-held phone or electronic device while driving. Drivers under 19 may not use a phone at all, even hands-free, except in an emergency.
concepts.tip: Hands on the wheel, phone away.

concepts.definition: Leave more following distance on wet roads. If you hydroplane, ease off the gas and keep the wheel straight until the tires grip again.
concepts.tip: Water on the road: ease off, steer straight.

concepts.definition: Check blind spots by turning your head before changing lanes. Give a motorcycle a full lane, and leave extra following distance behind it.
concepts.tip: A motorcycle gets a whole lane.

points: Signal 100 feet before a turn in town and 200 feet outside town.
Headlights on from sunset to sunrise and when wipers are needed.
Dim high beams within 500 feet of oncoming cars and 300 feet of cars ahead.
Parking lights never replace headlights.
No hand-held phone use while driving.

summary: Illinois uses graduated licensing so that new drivers build skill step by step. This chapter covers the instruction permit, the practice hours, and the night and passenger limits for young drivers.

You can get an instruction permit at 15 if you are enrolled in an approved driver education course. With a permit, you must drive with a licensed adult who is at least 21 years old. Drivers under 18 must hold the permit for at least 9 months and complete 50 hours of supervised driving, including 10 hours at night, before getting a license.

Drivers under 18 may not drive from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. Sunday through Thursday nights, or from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. Friday and Saturday nights, and breaking this rule may lead to a suspension. For the first 12 months with a license, or until age 18 if sooner, a driver under 18 may carry only one passenger under 20, not counting brothers, sisters, children, or stepchildren. Drivers under 19 may not use a cell phone while driving, even hands-free, except in an emergency.
The written test has at least 35 questions, and you must answer 80% correctly to pass, which is 28 of 35.

concepts.definition: Available at 15 with enrollment in an approved driver education course. You must drive with a licensed adult who is at least 21.
concepts.tip: 15 to start, and always with an adult 21 or older.

source.org: Illinois Rules of the Road (Illinois Secretary of State)

concepts.definition: Hold the permit at least 9 months and complete 50 hours of supervised driving, including 10 hours at night.
concepts.tip: 9 months, 50 hours, 10 at night.

concepts.definition: Drivers under 18 may not drive from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. Sunday through Thursday nights, or from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. Friday and Saturday nights. Breaking the rule may lead to a suspension.
concepts.tip: School nights 10, weekend nights 11, home by then until 6.

source.org: Illinois Rules of the Road (Illinois Secretary of State)

concepts.definition: For the first 12 months with a license, or until 18 if sooner, a driver under 18 may carry only one passenger under 20. Brothers, sisters, children, and stepchildren of the driver do not count.
concepts.tip: Year one: one young friend.

concepts.definition: At least 35 questions. You must answer 80% correctly, which is 28 of 35.
concepts.tip: Miss no more than 7.

points: Instruction permit at 15 with driver education enrollment.
Under 18: hold the permit 9 months and log 50 hours, 10 at night.
Under 18: no driving 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. Sunday to Thursday, 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. Friday and Saturday.
First 12 months: only one passenger under 20, family excepted.
Under 19: no phone at all while driving, except emergencies.

summary: This chapter covers how alcohol and drugs affect driving and the Illinois laws that can cost you your license. The rules are different for drivers under 21 and for adults, so learn both.

Alcohol slows your reactions and weakens your judgment, vision, and coordination, even after one drink. A 12-ounce beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine, and a 1.5-ounce shot of liquor each hold about the same amount of alcohol. Only time lowers the alcohol in your body. Prescription medicine, over-the-counter medicine, and cannabis can also impair you, and you can be charged with DUI for driving while impaired by them.

A driver 21 or older with a BAC of 0.08% or more is legally under the influence. Illinois has zero tolerance for drivers under 21: any trace of alcohol means losing driving privileges. For a driver under 21, a first failed test brings a 3-month suspension and a first refusal brings 6 months.

Under implied consent, by driving in Illinois you have agreed to a chemical test if you are arrested for DUI. For an adult first offender, failing the test brings a 6-month suspension and refusing it brings 12 months. This statutory summary suspension takes effect on the 46th day after the notice is given.

concepts.definition: A driver 21 or older with a BAC of 0.08% or more is legally under the influence.
concepts.tip: Adults: 0.08.

concepts.definition: A driver under 21 with any trace of alcohol loses driving privileges. A first failed test brings a 3-month suspension, and a first refusal brings 6 months.
concepts.tip: Under 21: zero means zero.

concepts.definition: Driving in Illinois means you have agreed to a chemical test if arrested for DUI. For an adult first offender, failing brings a 6-month suspension and refusing brings 12 months. The suspension starts on the 46th day after notice.
concepts.tip: Refuse the test, lose your license for a year.

concepts.definition: Alcohol slows reactions and weakens judgment and vision. Only time lowers BAC. Coffee, a cold shower, or fresh air do not sober you up.
concepts.tip: Only time sobers you up.

concepts.definition: Prescription medicine, over-the-counter medicine, and cannabis can impair driving. A prescription does not make impaired driving legal.
concepts.tip: Read the label before you drive.

points: Adult legal limit: BAC 0.08%.
Under 21: any trace of alcohol means losing driving privileges.
Adult first offender: 6 months for failing, 12 months for refusing.
Under 21, first time: 3 months for failing, 6 months for refusing.
Only time lowers your BAC.
